planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or set out container plants after the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; almost always propagated by cuttings since seed germination is slow and unreliable.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC IF INGESTED — site it away from areas where livestock, pets, or small children graze on foliage, and never burn the trimmings, since the smoke carries toxic compounds. Root cuttings in spring or set out container plants after the soil has warmed, in ordinary well-drained soil in full sun; oleander shrugs off heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil, which is why it lines highway medians and beachfront properties across the Gulf Coast and Southern California. Clusters of single or double flowers in white, pink, red, salmon, or yellow appear almost continuously from late spring through fall on new wood, so prune lightly right after a bloom flush rather than in late winter. Cold snaps below the high teens can kill it to the ground in zone 8, but established plants typically resprout vigorously from the root crown.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun, ideally with some shelter from hard freezes.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun, ideally with some shelter from hard freezes; Geiger tree is native to beach dunes and coastal hammocks of South Florida and the Caribbean and is exceptionally salt- and wind-tolerant, making it a signature small tree of Florida Keys and coastal landscaping. Clusters of crepe-textured, brilliant orange-red flowers appear nearly year-round in frost-free areas, followed by white, pear-shaped fruit that birds relish, while the large, rough, sandpapery leaves give the plant a distinctive tropical texture. It can be maintained as a large multi-trunked flowering shrub with occasional pruning or allowed to grow into a small canopy tree. Protect young plants from temperatures below the high 20s F, since it is one of the more cold-tender salt-tolerant natives available.

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; nick or scarify the hard seed coat before sowing if starting from seed.

directions: Set out container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; unlike the tree-form orchid trees (Bauhinia variegata and purpurea), this species is a loose, sprawling, non-invasive shrub with a scrambling habit that can be left informal as a mounding hedge or tied to a fence or trellis for a more vertical effect. Brick-red to orange, orchid-shaped flowers open in flushes from late spring through fall and draw butterflies and hummingbirds reliably. It thrives on neglect once established, tolerating heat, poor soil, and extended dry spells, and its twin-lobed leaves give it a soft, ferny texture even when not in bloom. Where winters dip into the low 20s F it dies back hard but usually resprouts from the base the following spring.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in fall or early spring in very well-drained, lean, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; scarify seed for faster, more even germination if starting from seed.

directions: Plant container-grown stock in fall or early spring in very well-drained, lean, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; this Trans-Pecos native thrives in exactly the hot, dry, alkaline conditions that defeat most flowering trees. Fragrant, powder-puff, golden-yellow flower balls cover the fine, mimosa-like bipinnate foliage in flushes from spring through fall, especially after summer rain, drawing bees and butterflies, and the plant is unarmed (thornless), unlike mesquite or acacia. It is usually grown as a large multi-stemmed shrub or small specimen tree and is extremely drought tolerant once established, needing supplemental water only the first year or two. Hard freezes can kill it to the ground, but it reliably resprouts from the root in spring.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in lean, gravelly or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; named selections are grown from cuttings rather than seed.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in lean, gravelly or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Lydia broom forms a low, cascading mound of fine blue-green stems that is smothered in brilliant golden-yellow pea-shaped flowers for several weeks in late spring. It is exceptionally well suited to spilling over rock walls, covering dry slopes, or edging a gravel bed, and unlike some brooms it stays naturally tidy and compact without aggressive reseeding. Good drainage is essential — it declines quickly in heavy clay or soil that stays wet — but once sited correctly it needs almost no irrigation or fertilizer.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings of a male, non-seeding cultivar such as 'Centennial' in spring in any well-drained soil in full sun; unselected female plants can seed aggressively and are best avoided in cultivated landscapes.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings of a male, non-seeding cultivar such as 'Centennial' in spring in any well-drained soil in full sun; desert broom is a broom-like, nearly leafless southwestern native shrub of green, rush-like stems that photosynthesize year-round, giving it an evergreen effect in the low desert. Male plants produce inconspicuous cream flowers in fall that feed late-season pollinators, while unselected female plants can seed aggressively and are best avoided in cultivated landscapes. It tolerates extreme heat, poor caliche or disturbed soil, and long dry spells with no supplemental water once roots are established, making it a workhorse screening or bank-stabilization shrub in Arizona and West Texas xeriscapes.
